But perhaps this child had been killed someplace else, maybe by a Serbian shell but maybe by a shell of the BH army, and this child was used in that way in order to prove a crime while the perpetrator had not been identified. And this bomb, which was known as "sow," could only make so much damage as the animal can make the mess.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job was not to go on the scene on my initiative. You say that somebody forced me to do that. The hierarchy is well known. My duty was to conduct an investigation. I had been informed, it was the job of an investigating judge to set up a team. I wasn't being manipulated. Nobody told me to do this or do that; photograph this or photograph that. I marked the physical evidence with numbers, and I explained what I found on the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, of course, the procedure in this Court is a mixed procedure. It mixes common law and civil law; it mixes both systems. So what you're doing might be acceptable, but as far as I'm concerned, I mean, this witness is under oath. He is a policeman, an investigator. When a crime has been made committed, he does his job. He goes on site to do his job. And you, as a Defence counsel, you're entitled, of course, to challenge his findings, but when you are saying that he lied, that he was sent by the authorities to make up -- to make up something, you know, for ideological reasons, you have a right to say this but you have to prove it. And if I look at the transcript and what you've said so far, you are always repeating that he's lying, that he was working for -- that everything was staged and so on. But so far I have seen no evidence to back all this, to back that he was working under orders and that he was working for an ideology. As a policeman, he's doing his job, his investigation. It might be that the bodies that he inspected might have been planted there. I don't know by what force. Maybe he doesn't even know about it. But he is under oath. Your job is to prove all this. If you just repeat this, we're not going anywhere. And it was a comment I wanted to the make, because, remember, this is a witness who is under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, look, what I wanted to hear from him was an explanation for some obvious things, and he failed to provide this explanation. I still maintain that the bomb that hit the television building and this incident as well was a fabrication that can easily be proven. I attended a trial as amicus curiae, and by His Honour Mr. Robinson I had been cautioned on a few occasions that I have to ask the question directly if I want to challenge the credibility of this witness, and that I was expected to clearly state my position. What I've learned over the years in this court is that I find it very difficult to say to someone that they are lying. I had almost been thrown out of the courtroom in Sombor when I told the witness that he was lying. If I am denied the possibility in this court, where I have been acting for about two years, to say to the witness that he was lying, if I had any powers, this witness should not have been allowed to leave this court because he was obstructing justice. Obstructing justice, preventing justice, is a serious crime. This kind of manipulation is also a serious crime that is punishable everywhere in the world. During this examination, and it seems that I'm going to prolong it, it seems that he told a lie so many times, and I will demonstrate this to you. Therefore, I'm compelled to say and use this word, although I find it very difficult, to call him a liar. I kindly ask Your Honours to trust me on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we understand each other. But my concern is that I want to have a demonstration of what you are putting forth. Just stating it is not enough. We need to have it backed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then maybe I should just sit down. It seems that I didn't ask any relevant question. Maybe I should sit down if you believe that my sole intention is to call this witness a liar. And he, indeed, is lying and I'm going to repeat this as many times as necessary. That is what I learned in this court, and I think that's an excellent thing, that when someone is not telling the truth, to tell them that they are lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the record, the statement attributed to me was Judge Mindua's. That's the last statement from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe, Your Honours, Mr. Robinson didn't read everything. I know what I said. In order not to be accused of politicising, but it is true that this kind of stage-managing was the reason that compelled the international community to interfere eventually and this witness took part in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's not waste time. If you have nothing more to cross-examine on, let us terminate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I am going to use half the time that the Prosecutor used, and I'm going to skip many questions that I originally intended to ask. I'm not going to ask any irrelevant questions that are not going to be beneficial to these proceedings. Now I will kindly ask for a document to be displayed. Let me first close this. Before I move on to this question, but it deals with the same topic and it has to do with the statement that he had given many years ago and which is going to be the backbone of my further cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But before that, Mr. Witness, after what we have heard, the BH army or the BH police also had these air bombs known as "sows" at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But they also had proper aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about a meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Supreme Command? And I will present this when the time comes. There was a conversation between Izetbegovic and Silajdzic, they were virtually completing with each other, and Izetbegovic was boasting, precisely at the time when this offensive was ongoing, that the army had manufactured 800 bombs. Since the indictment claims that the army of Republika Srpska was the only one who had these bombs, I would like to ask you if you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have to present a document that I have in my hands, which is being translated. I had asked for it to be urgently translated, but I didn't receive it yet. The number is DD00-0403. There is no signature on this document, and it's written in B/C/S. Can we please have it on our monitors. Let us move on to page 1. This is a document dated the 12th of August, 1994. Two days before that date, General Dragomir Milosevic took over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And if you can follow this document on your screen, you will see that this is a military document signed by Brigadier General Enver Hadzihasanovic. It says here that it was received on file of the BH army and certified by the BH army. In this letter, it shows that an enormous quantity of weapons was being forwarded to the 1st Corps. Let me read a couple of things from this letter just to see whether you know anything about that. If you don't know, just say so. And if you can give me very brief answers, preferably yes or no. Do you understand me, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Strictly confidential. Considerable successes of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the last two months." Can you see that, sir, at the very beginning, at the top?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do, below the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then it goes on to say: "In order to present these results," et cetera, et cetera, I will not read any further, "the territories that have been freed," et cetera. Look at this bullet 2 or dash 2: "According to available information, 300 soldiers had been killed by the Chetniks." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The second item?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says different. You said that they were killed by Chetniks but I don't see this word.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But what does this "SCA" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 305 SCA army -- soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which means that the BH army had killed 305 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm allowed to read this. I see this document for the first time. It doesn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the reason why I'm asking you this is as follows: A large quantity of ammunition was seized and it was being forwarded to the 1st Corps; is that true? It says it was forwarded to the 1st Corps. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The 1st Corps, we are forwarding to you the summary."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now, we come to a whole list of document -- of weapons being forwarded, but I'm asking you about the first item, tank T34, but it says then "Maljutka rocket" and then a launcher for a Maljutka rocket. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the BH army also had weapons. You said that they didn't have aerial bombs, but it seems that they did have Maljutka rockets and launchers for these rockets. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just read what I see in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look what they forwarded to the 1st Corps. It says a Maljutka rocket and a launcher for this rocket.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can find it elsewhere, but can you tell me, based on this, is it fair to say that the BH army had certain rockets, although these were wire-guided rockets. But does it mean that at that point in time, on the 12th of August, the BH army had rockets and launchers at their disposal? I'm asking you this because the indictment says that it was only the army of Republika Srpska who had these rockets and these launchers for specific weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-0403, may the document please be marked for identification. Thank you. It still needs to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It does not seem as if we'll be getting more than 100 pages of translations per month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is relatively short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the reference number D34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I have this difficult moment approaching where I have to give references for the B/C/S and for the English at the same time. I have prepared well. I will try to be as effective as possible. I have the statement of this witness here. The 15th of November, 1995, that's the date. DD00-0440. This is a document that was produced before the war was even over, or maybe it was. No, it wasn't. No, because Dragomir Milosevic is indicted -- stands indicted of crimes committed up to the 21st of November. I just want the witness to confirm for us if he provided this statement, DD00-0440, and then I can start examining him in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to ensure that the monitor is not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm assured by the court deputy that it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If the witness can please just confirm whether this is a document that he signed, whether he provided this statement on the 15th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it, and I provided the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If page 1 is not being displayed outside the courtroom, I would like to move to page 2 of this document. And if we can then go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see your statement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So there, if you look at page 1, the very first sentence, you say: "Before that I finished a special course for forensic technology. My original profession was a mechanical technician."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "After a period of practice with more experienced colleagues, I began to work independently in November 1993." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I dealt with all kinds of crimes, including crimes against property, murders, and other kinds of serious crimes, such as those related to genocide." Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Crime investigations. I think it's a poor translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Investigations related to genocide." We can look at the English, but that's what the Serbian version says, what you signed. But even as early as 1993, you were dealing with investigations related to genocide.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in the security services centre, a special department was set up that we called the genocide department. As for the shellings and everything else that I investigated, we just subsumed the whole thing under genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the very next sentence. "I only worked in the Sarajevo area." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then: "I worked on 350 different cases, 52 of them related to genocide." What sort of a genocide was perpetrated back in 1993? What was the genocide, and what were the cases that you described as genocide? And based on just what? And do you know what the word means at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked 350 different cases, including the incidents of burglary and that sort of thing. Fifty-two cases were cases where I went to the scene and had to do with sniping and shelling and everything that began in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this done pursuant to orders by your superiors, again? Because as soon as 1993 the BH government was already filing its criminal report for genocide. Did this have to do with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it had nothing to do with that. This was from 1995, and by this time a lot was known already. Many people had been killed; many people had been wounded; many people had been displaced. So this was a statement that I provided back in 1995. Nobody foisted it on me and nobody forced my hand to say anything at all, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did spend a lot of time on investigations which involved casualties, quite regardless of the war, if my understanding is accurate. It wasn't just bomb victims. It wasn't just victims of the war. You were also involved very often in dealing with manslaughter, murder, that sort of thing, homicide. Isn't that the case, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, over 350 such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have the title page of a newspaper displayed on our screens. This is not a Belgrade-based newspaper. It is not an American newspaper. It is a Sarajevo newspaper; it's a Bosniak newspaper, dated last summer. This is something that this newspaper published. This is DD00-0438. It's the front page of the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There you go. That's the photograph. This is a newspaper called "Free Bosnia," a Bosniak paper, if you like, a Muslim paper, whatever you wish to call it. I don't really distinguish along those lines myself. You see what it says, don't you? "SB Discovers the Horrific Fate of Serbs in Sarajevo - 850 Serbs Killed." There are documents about that in the possession of the OTP; I know that for a fact. Did you conduct -- [French on English channel] -- and throw into caldrons or into the river? Did you have any investigation like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted on-site investigations. I did not conduct the investigation at Kazina. I don't remember a single body being thrown into the river. All of my on-site investigations throughout that period were recorded, and you can find them in the files of the Sarajevo canton. It's no secret. You can go there and you can find them. Everything that I did is well documented. I don't remember any specific cases. There were crimes committed by criminals. I did investigate cases of murder. There were all sorts of names cropping up, Bosnian names, Serb names, Croat names. Sarajevo is a multi-ethnic city. And this is not a Bosniak paper, it's a Bosnian paper, if you see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a Sarajevo-based paper; right? It's not a Belgrade-based paper. It's a Bosnian paper; right? That's what it says. "Shocking Photographs of Atrocities and Murder," that's what it says. That's what it says. There's a lot more than just that going on, but at least 850 is something that nobody ever challenged, is it? Were you in charge of any of these investigations? Did you investigate a single murder like that, a single killing like that? And what do you really know about it, since you were a homicide investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a forensic technician. I worked over 350 cases, on-site investigations, at the time. There are records; you can check that. All the dates are there. So I don't know. I had nothing to do with the horrific fate of Serbs in Sarajevo, as the front page says. I did do on-site investigations. You asked me about Kazina. I don't know. I can't remember all the names. You said this was a Bosniak paper, not that it was a Bosnian paper, and that's what my objection was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are three notations on the record where the interpreters have asked that you both slow down in the interests of the interpretation. You're speaking too fast, overlapping. Please observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it says here "Free Bosnia," so this is a Bosniak paper, a Muslim paper, or isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a newspaper produced in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's not a Bosniak paper; it's not a Muslim-only paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Serbs always speak of Republika Srpska. They never said that. But, okay, have you seen this or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First time I have set eyes on it. Normally I don't read this particular newspaper, if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be skipping a lot of questions again. I'll be moving to the snipers now. I will try not to dwell on anything that is insubstantial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You talked about snipers; it's page 4 of the English, paragraph 1, the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, no, we have a new one. I'll be re-tendering it probably. DD00-0440. This document is no longer ... It's page 4 of the English, paragraph 1. B/C/S, the reference is page 6, paragraph 2. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You can see paragraph 2 of that statement, sir, can't you? You dealt with snipers, and yesterday you explained about particular sniping incidents. I'll just refer to some of the questions already asked by the Judges. In your capacity as an expert, you say this: "A sniping investigation resembles a classical murder investigation. By sniping, I mean a fire-arm with an optical device. Of course I investigated cases without knowing if the perpetrator had used an optical device or not." What about the majority of cases that were involved in in your capacity as investigator? Did you not believe in most cases that a telescope or this optical device had been used? First of all, what you say here, is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my statement. I never knew nor was I able to see whether an optical device had been used or not. What I would normally see was bodies or bullet marks, but I would never see the weapon itself. As for the snipers themselves, all of the places in the city were well known that were covered by snipers. The phrase used was "Sniper fire: Watch out, don't go there." Of course we couldn't see if it was actually a sniping rifle. And the kind of rifle used for sniping normally has an optical device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you must ask your questions directly and without the long introductory remarks. Just get to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wanted to hear whether the witness could confirm his statement. That was my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true, what you said in your statement in relation to this weapon with an optical device?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what a sniping rifle is. It's a rifle with an optical device.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to show the witness 65 ter document number 738, page 3. 65 ter number 738, page 3. You can see the witness's name, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Show it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Show him what it is that you wish him to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is a report that you worked on. You were shown it yesterday, about the snipers, by the OTP, and the Chamber was much interested in these documents and the sniping incidents. There was talk of the plastic sheeting that was used to cover the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you what the document says and then we can go back into closed session later on, perhaps. You can later have a look in closed session what I'm showing him. That course of action is for the Chamber, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is -- and I think she was killed. Semka Kozadra, we talked about her a lot yesterday, didn't we? I can read that for him and then he can have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it that you wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to show him the sheets that he talked about on house windows, where some women were wounded and one was even killed. It's the sheeting that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, when Kozadra Semka was killed on the 3rd of March, 1995. So down the middle of that paragraph, it says: "When an on-site investigation was carried out" - and it was carried out by the witness - "it was established that the bullet had torn through the blanket that was on the balcony and then the sheet. So first it tore through the blanket. "Blanket" in our language means just what it means, blanket. So this is no sheeting, no plastic sheet. It was a blanket hung across the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, was there a blanket on that window or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the blanket was in the window and there was a plastic sheet, as I explained yesterday. I explained everything yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now there's another document presented to you yesterday, 65 ter 738, pages 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What use have you made of this document? It's not clear to me what question you have put to the witness on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on this document, if he said that there was first a blanket, then it means that no one can see into the flat through a thick blanket. Nothing can be seen going on through the blanket. There was a plastic sheet before it, but before that was a blanket that could not be seen through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't put any question to him yet. I mean, you're making submissions on the basis of the document, but it is not clear to me what question you're putting to the witness. This is not the time to make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, then I'm not very good at putting questions. This is what he established in his report. There was a blanket covering the window and the bullet passed through the blanket. That's what he says. Is it true that the window was covered with a blanket? Is it correct, what he established here? I don't know what it says in the English version. If the translation is bad, then it's something that must not have happened, because in this original report compiled in the Serbian language, it says that there was a plastic sheet but that the window was covered with a blanket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in the report that it wasn't on the window, it was at the balcony, on the terrace. That's where the blanket was. And the living-room window had a plastic sheet. This blanket served as visual protection, not the protection from light, as a kind of curtain to prevent people seeing what is going on in the flat. The bullet went through the blanket, through the window, through the plastic sheet on the door and then hit the woman in the hip. She was just going out of the bathroom. She wasn't killed; she was just wounded. It says very clear that it first went through the blanket on the balcony, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the whole balcony was covered with a blanket. But the whole balcony was covered with a blanket, enclosed with the blanket, precisely in order to prevent anyone seeing what is happening there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I don't know how you arrived at this assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say here the whole balcony was covered with a blanket and no one can see anything from outside.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is correct, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only purpose was to prevent anyone seeing into it, but it allowed light to come on top and on the sides. It only covered the view towards Dobrinja 4 from where the bullet had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you maintain that the sniper was precisely targeting the target that was behind this blanket. Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting for the interpretation in order not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bullet flew through the blanket and through the sheet. I cannot say that the lady was targeted intentionally. However, the flat where she was was intentionally targeted and hit. I never said that she was intentionally shot. But this window and the blanket protecting the window was targeted intentionally, and the result was the wounding of this lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this answer, but please look at the document that was read out to you yesterday by the Prosecutor. It's 65 ter document 738, pages 5 and 6. It again deals with this unfortunate woman, Semka Kozadra. I'm going to read out to you and ask you to confirm it because you signed this document. Can you see this? Let me read it to you. This is what your report says: "On the 3rd of March, 1995, at around 0745 hours, in a ground floor flat, on number 6 Emila Zole Street, Semka Kozadra was wounded. The wounded was caused by a stray bullet of 7.62-millimetre passing through the blanket that served as a visual protection at the balcony." And then you go on with other details. Please, is this true, what you say, that this stray bullet came from somewhere else? Is this correct, what you say in your report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The bullet arrived, and I recorded its path.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it was a stray bullet. You immediately came to that conclusion because there was this blanket, et cetera, that this was not an intended target?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't up to me to determine whether it was done intentionally or not, but I did say that the blanket was hit from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the last sentence you say: "The bullet came from the direction of Dobrinja 4, which is under the control of the aggressor." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have a stray bullet, and Dobrinja, which is at the heart of Sarajevo, was equally populated by Serbs and Bosniaks. How could you say that it had come from Dobrinja? Dobrinja was Dobrinja. Whether it was Dobrinja 4, 5, or 6 is irrelevant. Why did you say that it came from the aggressor positions? It was a stray bullet. Can you please explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted this investigation, and the only thing you can see through the window of this room was the Dobrinja 4 neighbourhood, which at the time was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the BH army was also there, because they shared the same positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know that. I know that the Republika Srpska army was there. I used to live in Dobrinja 4. I was expelled from my flat, and I know this neighbourhood perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you also know very well that the distance between the two positions in places were 10 to 15 metres, sometimes 50 metres. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you regarding the positions that there probably was a ring surrounding Sarajevo by both armies. I said that it came from the direction of Dobrinja 4. I didn't specify the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that could be the position of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but equally it could have been the position of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building was on the very front line. I don't think there were any trenches there, and that nobody could maintain them, because this building was on the very demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the front line passed through many buildings; that on the one side you had members of the BH army and on the other side there were member -- or the other part of the building there were members of the army of Republika Srpska. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Neighbourhoods were divided. It was like it was, and unfortunately this woman had no option but to live where she lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to finish this topic of sniping, I would like to refer you to another document mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the killing of Zineta Sinanovic. This woman was definitely killed. It happened on the 3rd of March. It's 65 ter number 738, page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this statement? We discussed it yesterday. I'm going to read to you the penultimate paragraph. "I would like to say that on the same day," which means on the 3rd of March, and the same time, "it was noticed that bullets entered flats on higher floors but there were no casualties." Is this what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a part of the town which was divided by the front line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say which building we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, is that one of the buildings that the front line was passing through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at what it says further on. "The building where we live partially faces Dobrinja 4 neighbourhood which was under the aggressor's control." And it ends like this: "In the rooms facing this part of the neighbourhood are uninhabited." Is this correct, what it says here in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm what is written here, but I cannot say whether anyone lived in them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And I am putting to you that that was precisely the reason, because they were facing the front and because there was constant fear that people will be shooting at each other, that bullets could be -- could be stray, and that as a result many people were victims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did this on-site investigation. I noted that this woman was shot in this flat. My duty was to document where the bullet had come from, whether there was any deaths caused, and to prepare a report. Of course there were casualties. People were killed by stray bullets, by intentional targeting. There was shooting everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely what I wanted to ask you. All these people that were killed on the side which was under the control of the BH army were portrayed as sniper incident victims, which means that they were targets of riflemen who had rifles with devices or with any other weapons, but these were intentional shootings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. Some people were killed by stray bullets. People were being killed by snipers while they were running across the streets. I myself had to run away from the snipers when I tried to cross the street because people in civilian clothes crossing the streets were particularly targeted by snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the documents that I have already, you -- and these are indisputable documents that I'm going to present to this Court, you note that shots had been fired by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in the range of 10 to 15.000 a day. Of course that applies to the Serbian side as well. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was war. There was shooting. I don't know which side fired how many -- the number of bullets that each side had fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can possibly complete in about 10 or 15 minutes, if we could have the break now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to have a break a while ago, because I intended originally to tender these documents into evidence: First of all, DD00-0440; that's the statement made by this witness on the 15th of November, 1995. And then the front page of "Slobodna Bosna," or "Free Bosnia," number DD00-0438. Then 65 ter 738, pages 3 and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In future, I'd prefer you to deal with the question of admission right after, when the document is fresh in our minds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit the statement of 15th November; that's the statement of the witness. Yes. Now, the other two, just describe them. What do they deal with, those two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can show you the other documents. One is DD00-0438; that's the front the page of "Slobodna Bosna" magazine. It speaks about -- I wouldn't like to repeat that again. I'm going to hand over the entire magazine in translation when it becomes required. I think that it's not necessary at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This magazine has no connection with the witness. There's no relationship established and we see no basis for admitting it. We'll not admit it. What's the third one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's, in fact, two documents. They are both contained in 65 ter 738. The first document is page 3, and the second document is page 13. These are the documents that speak about sniping incidents in which the witness was involved in investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the document contained in number 738 under 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May it be shown on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the two documents that describe this blanket, the stray bullet, et cetera. That's the two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And where did it emanate from?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 65 ter document number 738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I meant who made the document? Whose document is it? Is this a Novi Grad public security station, crime police department? You say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't. It says -- there's the witness's name and it says that he was involved there. Yeah, yeah. That's what it says at the top of the document, but from the document we can see that the witness was involved in the investigation. And also the second document was prepared -- or, rather, an investigation was conducted by this witness, and they were all produced as a result of his on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am of the understanding that the document produced by the witness has already been admitted into evidence during my examination. But in any event, if the first one is going to be admitted, I would ask that it's admitted under seal, if his name is on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This document has already been admitted in your examination-in-chief; is that what you're saying? Can the court deputy confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The document that I see on the screen, it is my understanding that it has been admitted. And the document that he himself has signed has been admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can you give us the information of the P number that was given to this second document, the Novi Grad Public Security Station Official Note.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I am able to do that. Firstly, the one that he himself completed was Exhibit P150, under seal; and then the next document is Exhibit P151, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're not going to do that now. That's an administrative exercise. The Prosecutor says it was admitted. The court deputy will check on it. In any event, it's a document that would be admitted. So the administrators can determine that and report to us as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness statement dated 15 November 1995 will become Exhibit D35, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So let us move on. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before my last topic, there is just one thing that I would like to show the witness. It's about the bus that he mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember mentioning a bus yesterday, and the glass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right if I said that you conducted that on-site investigation without the actual bus? And the wounded had been taken away. The only basis for you to go on was the shattered glass; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted an on-site investigation in two different places. The first place was the place where the bus was and the other place was the place where the bus had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you conducted your investigation without the actual bus, didn't you? You investigated it based on the shards of glass alone that you found at the scene; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conducted it on the spot after the bus was found in the Dobrinja neighbourhood. We went back to the place where the bus had been hit, and the bus was not returned there, so we did that particular scene without the presence of the bus, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the third time: It was only based on the shattered glass that you found on the spot; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found splinters and shattered glass on that spot, but we came there to begin with because witnesses had told us to go there and told us that that was where the bus had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on those bits of shattered glass, you concluded where the bullet had come from; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another thing: Do you know where Mojmilo is? It's the long ridge. It's 3 kilometres long. It overlooks Sarajevo in its entirety, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where that hill is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it 3 kilometres long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite long. I'm not sure if it's 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: May as well be two and a half. Is it not true that throughout the war it was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The side facing Alipasino Polje, that particular neighbourhood, was the site that was, throughout, controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But there were parts of Mojmilo that were held by the army of Republika Srpska. Is that what you're claiming, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The side facing Lukavica and Trebevic was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But what about at the foot of that hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which side do you mean, the north side or the south side?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Both sides. I mean the side facing the Serb positions and the side facing the BH army positions. The army of Republika Srpska was at the foot of Mojmilo, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on the west side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. They were at the foot of the hill. They weren't close to the peak, were they? They were down on the lower slopes of the hill, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is I wasn't supposed to go there. I wasn't allowed to go there. I'm not sure if they were higher up or lower down at the foot of it. What I do know is that, as far as this side of Mojmilo was concerned, I was free to walk around without the risk of being hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In a way you are saying that up there in the hill, in some way the army of Republika Srpska held certain positions. Did they hold any positions at all up there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't venture that far. What I know is that I was free to walk around safely, so there was no firing from the south side of that hill, the side facing Alipasino Polje. It's easier for me if I use the cardinal points, if I talk about the northern side, the southern side. If you say "the foot of a hill," that means nothing at all to me. It could be south, north, east or west.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we say that it was from near the peak of that hill that the area under the BH army control was surveyed? And that's why you were never hit and that's why you were never fired at. Whereas the other side facing the Serb positions and Lukavica was under the control of those who also occupied the very peak of that hill. And it's a ridge that is 3 kilometres long, overlooking Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago that the side facing Alipasino Polje, or, rather, the north side, was under the control of the BH army. The other side was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. I don't know specifically where their respective positions were, because I never went that far myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's a sufficient explanation, indeed, a very good explanation. I'm thankful for your opinion, as a matter of fact. Can you just tell me about the bus that was within the area of responsibility of the BH army. Was it exactly at the foot of that hill, the hill that was under the control and within the area of responsibility of the BH army? Isn't that where it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was heading down the 9th Transversal Road towards Western Dobrinja, and this is the western slope of the hill. The bus was above the Olympic village of Mojmilo and it was hit before it reached the Olympic village, at a junction between Mojmilo B and Mojmilo C, which is the crossing of these two streets, the 9th Transversal and Safeta Hadzica Street. That is the western slope of Mojmilo and it is still very much a slope. You certainly couldn't call it the foot of that particular hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't have much left to go. Before I launch into my next set of questions, let me ask you this: The Zagreb Hotel, which used to be a hotel before the war, needless to say, during the war, became the headquarters -- or, rather, at least there were lots of police there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. What about the Belgrade Hotel, which was also very central? I think the police administration was based there. At least you could know that, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that this was a police building. I probably would have known if it had been. In fact, I'm sure I would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I assume that at least you can tell me, if it was neither the Belgrade Hotel nor the Zagreb Hotel, where, then, was the central police administration, the central wartime police administration in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP building and the security services centre building, those were the police buildings. As for police stations, they were still in the same place as they always were, even before the war; across the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There were plenty of those and there were a lot of police there and they were armed at least with pistols, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the security services centres, the BH MUP, and the police stations; the Centar police station, Bijeljina police station, Nova Sarajevo police station, Novi Grad police station, Ilidza police station, which was at Hrastica. I never carried out any on-site investigations there because there was another colleague of mine working there. So the ones that I've just listed for you, those were the police stations that I was familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us, roughly speaking, how many police stations there were? That's my first question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have listed the ones that I was aware of at the time. I don't know if any other police stations that actually existed that were used at the time. I have given you all I know. Centar, Bijeljina, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, those are the police stations where I carried out on-site investigations, as well as Stari Grad. I don't know of any other police stations that may or may not have existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Marin Dvor, which is a name that crops up a lot in this trial and which is a place that happens to be near the tallest sky-scrapers down your side? How far is Marin Dvor from the two tallest sky-scrapers in Sarajevo itself? Marin Dvor. Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a police station at Marin Dvor; it's still there. And the only thing that separates the police station from the sky-scrapers is the so-called Trscanska Street, which is about 15 metres wide, plus the pavements on either side of the street, which produces a total of 50 metres at the very most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you know about this. I assume that you should. It was from those really tall sky-scrapers, the two tallest sky-scrapers, that sniper fire would be opened at their own citizens; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not something that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you know that snipers use those locations a lot to target positions held at the time by the army of Republika Srpska. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Those two sky-scrapers were often targeted by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that both sky-scrapers were smashed up and all the glass panes were gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact - and I'm talking about the police most of all - that it was from those sniper nests and those buildings that the greatest number of civilians were killed on the other side, the side that was at the time held by the army of Republika Srpska? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about the fact that those two buildings were targeted for that specific reason alone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that between 15.000 and 20.000 policemen were under arms? They had pistols, rifles, mortars. Are you familiar with that particular bit of information, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the police had weapons. They had pistols and some had machine-guns, but I don't know about any of them having mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that there were so many armed policemen, do you perhaps know that the 1st Corps at no point in time numbered less than 60.000 soldiers? The 12th Division itself had about 50.000 armed soldiers, especially during the period that the indictment against General Milosevic refers to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unfamiliar with those facts and figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple of things left that I'd like to ask you in relation to the hills surrounding Sarajevo. The indictment claims that Serbs occupied the hills above Sarajevo and they never did anything else from those hills but target civilians for no reason at all. Do you agree with that, the Serbs being on those hills pounding Sarajevo from up there, the sole objective being to kill the odd civilian - a woman, a child, people fetching water, people growing vegetables in their garden to make ends meet? Was that the sole objective of the Serbian army, those people who were holding positions along the ridges around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked my opinion. I'll give you my opinion. As a matter of fact, I think so, the reason being this: I was stuck in Sarajevo that whole time. I couldn't get on with my life as a normal citizen. Once my duty, term, was over I couldn't leave Sarajevo. I was under constant threat, just as everyone else in Sarajevo was. I could have been killed; fortunately, I wasn't. I could have been wounded. I certainly was besieged in Sarajevo. The city was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were a police officer and you worked on the vital cases, the most vital of all cases, in fact; that is my understanding. A doctor was free to leave Sarajevo, for example, whenever he or she liked. They could have used the tunnel. How many times had you -- how many times did you use the tunnel beneath the Butmir airport, or did you never use the tunnel, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the tunnel once to leave to go and fetch food so that we could survive. I asked for leave; I got ten days. I used the tunnel because that was the only way out. It was the only way to get through to the other side. I'm not sure what the distance was. We would come back with supplies that sometimes lasted us no more than days. And that was the only time I used the tunnel, and this proves that was the only way out. And not everybody enjoyed the privilege of being able to use the tunnel. There were lots of us and there was only that one tunnel. You had to -- you had to squat. You had to bend your back to be able to walk through the tunnel; you couldn't just walk upright.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that full well that that is what it was like back in 1993 and for a while in 1994. It wasn't that easy to get through. But towards the end of 1994 and for the whole of 1995, there were actually tracks in the tunnel that were laid. And it was possible to use those tracks or rails, vehicles that were mounted on those rails, to bring supplies into the city or whatever the necessities were at the time. However, the tunnel was also continuously being used by the BH army to leave Sarajevo and to go back. Wasn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some rails that were laid in the tunnel. That's true. I remember passing through the tunnel. It wasn't just me. There were convoys of people inching their way in and out, all of those who had received permission to leave. You weren't just free to use the tunnel as you saw fit. You needed permission for that. I'll not sure who passed through the tunnel and when. I only did that once, when I wasn't on duty. I didn't, myself, keep track of any doctors or engineers or other military staff using the tunnel. Therefore, I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But there was no way for any of the 40.000 Serbs to use the tunnel unless they had paid big money. Some people did, in fact, pay up the money, the big money. They got through the tunnel and they were killed once they reached other side. What can you, an as investigator, tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you an answer to that. In my whole department throughout that whole period of time, the department was a multi-ethnic one - we had Serbs working for us - they would use the tunnel and they would soon be back alive. No one ever killed any of them just because their name happened to be a Serb one. I am not familiar of any cases where someone used a tunnel and was killed at the other end just because they happened to be Serbs. There were a lot of Serbs in Sarajevo who just continued to -- business as usual. I know plenty of them who never left Sarajevo during the war. And one thing I know for sure is that none of them were subjected to mistreatment. I talked to a lot of them. We went to shelters together. We tried to get on together all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that you have a lot of friends amongst Serbs, tell me at least one name of a Serb who managed to go out of Sarajevo and come back again, to be exposed to the hail of bullets? Just tell me that and I'm not going to tell you anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that entire battalions used to go out to other fronts, to Mount Igman and other battlefields all across Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The tunnel had been excavated, but I don't know about any such events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We mentioned Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask the witness, or can I ask you to ask the witness, a question of clarification? Because I did not understand fully whether the tunnel was used sometimes also by Serbs who wanted to leave Sarajevo and come back again. Can you ask that question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single Serb -- let's say a Serbian policemen, a colleague of yours, fine. But were there any women, children, ordinary citizens, not policemen or soldiers, although there were of course Serbs in Sarajevo who were soldiers and policemen? I'd like to hear from you, was there a child or a woman who managed to get out of Sarajevo and come back again to the place where she or he could have been killed? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you an example that I know of. I gave you one name of the man who went out and came back again. He was a Serb. As for women and children, I don't know. I didn't see any because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what I'm asking you. Do you know of a single ordinary citizen, most of all of women or children, going out of Sarajevo, being allowed to go out of Sarajevo, and come back, unless they paid a hefty sum of money. If they paid a lot of money, why would they go back to Sarajevo at all? Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any money being paid. I said I wasn't there. I don't know who went out. I didn't keep track of that, and I answered your question by saying I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I need not insist on this any longer. We're going to present additional evidence as well as the Prosecution will do. What do you about Mojmilo hill, which is 745 metres high? Who held positions on that hill? Were those positions of the BH army controlling the entire area of Grbavica, the Jewish cemetery, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a hill overlooking Sarajevo, where the line was. I never went up there and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're saying that there were also soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska on Mojmilo as well. Is that what you are claiming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything. That was one of the hills surrounding Sarajevo, and I knew when one -- when I walked around Sarajevo, I had to be wary of those hills. But I don't know where the exact positions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question on the translation, on line 10. [In English] You're saying that there were also soldiers of Republika Srpska on Mojmilo as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the point? Because we're hearing from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just a correction for the transcript, because it's not Mojmilo at line 10 -- line 11, but Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So at line 11, the reference to Mojmilo should be Debelo Brdo; is that correct? Is that correct, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. I am not following the transcript. I can't speak English, so I cannot look at the screen. I have no time for that. I asked the question about Mojmilo and that's where I left it off. Now I'm asking the witness about Debelo Brdo, which is the point that dominates the entire centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that this is where the positions of the army of Republika Srpska were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not saying that. I said that I didn't know. I never went up there, so I don't know who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Debelo Brdo is a place which dominates Marin Dvor and the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have a domineering -- a commanding view of the town from this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the allegation in the indictment that most shooting -- sniper shooting came from the Jewish cemetery, while this cemetery is at the foot of the Debelo Brdo? Would you care to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The city of Sarajevo is at the hill of Debelo Brdo. It's in the valley. And the Jewish cemetery is on the slopes of this hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colina Kapa, 940 metres high. It is somewhat to the west of Debelo Brdo. Trebevic is only 50 or 60 metres higher than Colina Kapa. The positions of BH army were also on Colina Kapa. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I simply cannot believe that, given the job that you were doing, but I will accept what you've just told me. I have a few more questions and then I'll finish. If we go to the north in the area of responsibility of BH army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying you're not aware of the positions held by the BH army in and around Sarajevo? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. I don't know where these positions exactly were because I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo and Mojmilo, were these hills in the area of responsibility of BH army? And these hills dominate Sarajevo and the centre of the town; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go there, and I cannot know where the positions of the BH army were or the positions of the army of Republika Srpska. I know that these hills surround the city of Sarajevo, but where these positions were, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The job that you have, would it be fair to describe it as a job in the security forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked for the security services centre, but my job was in town. It didn't involve the front line. I never went there. This name, security services centre, means police, actually, and that is the name taken from the earlier period when the police was part of the security services of the state. But I myself was in town all the time and I didn't go to the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I put my question very simply. I'm not asking you whether the BH army positions were there. I'm asking you in terms of geography. In the area of responsibility of the BH army, Mojmilo, Debelo Brdo and Colina Kapa, were they in the area of responsibility of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have exhausted that one now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your job, did you wear a uniform while you were on the job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The forensic technician goes to the scene for investigation in civilian clothes. However, in that period, the entire security services centre was issued with uniforms because we didn't have any clothes. Our clothes were worn and torn. We were issued these uniforms but we were not obliged to wear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not even as a child, you never went to Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo and Mojmilo. You never went to those places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do these three hills overlook Sarajevo from that side, if we disregard Trebevic as being slightly taller than -- higher than Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, these hills surround Sarajevo, and Sarajevo is in the valley surrounded by these hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I have exhausted this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have exhausted this topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, I just wanted to find out, you do know where the Serb positions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This question relating to the hills I don't know. I know that they were in Nedzarici, but I cannot identify exactly the houses. I know that they set up a ring around Sarajevo, but where it was exactly, whether it was 1, 2, or 3 kilometres, I really don't know. I never went to any positions of either of the sides. I can tell you, though, that Sarajevo was surrounded from all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you have given an abundance of evidence of bullets and shots and mortars coming from the Serb position, coming from the direction of the Serb position, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I did. But if you look at Sarajevo being surrounded, all the projectiles that arrived came from that position. I didn't say that they originated there, but they did come from this ring where the Serbian soldiers were. But I never said specifically from which location they had been firing. If you view Sarajevo as something in the centre, and then there were two rings around Sarajevo itself, I did say that they were coming from the direction where the Serbian soldiers were, and they were, in fact, there because Sarajevo was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event, your evidence is that you don't know where the BiH positions were in and around Sarajevo, even while you were a member of the security forces or services.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the criminal investigation department of the criminal investigation police. If there were other departments there, I wasn't part of them. I was part of the criminal investigation department, and I did the job that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I used the term "security forces" to cover both the army and the police. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have exhausted my questions concerning the southern side, but I still have some questions about the northern side. Therefore, I would like to ask the witness the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does he know that Zuc hill is 850 metres high, that it's on the northern side; that Orlic hill is about 876 metres high? And there are some other hills which I'm not going to mention now. They're all on -- to the north. And does he know that the BH army detachment held positions on all these hills?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript did not record "Zuc," which is 850 metres high; Orlic, 876 metres. As I said, there are other hills to the north of the approximate same height, at least five of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the BH army were on those hills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sokolje; Brijesce Brdo, to the west; Svabino Brdo, that's 700 metres, 689 to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The names have not been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sokolje; Brijesce Brdo; Svabino Brdo, 689 metres high. Again we don't have the names. I have to repeat this. I'll do it slowly. Sokolje neighbourhood, rather Sokolje hill; Brijesce hill; Svabino hill, 689 metres. On the one side, these overlook Rajlovac, which is on the Serb side, and on the other side they overlook the entire Sarajevo field, which is the very heart of Sarajevo. Do you know about that, and do you know about the fact that these positions, too, were being held at the time by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Brijesce Brdo. There's a settlement there with private homes. Sokolje is not a hill; it's a neighbourhood at the foot of Brijesce hill, facing Rajlovac. I also know that this is in the Novi Grad area, and that's where I conducted an on-site investigation when the neighbourhood of Brijesce Brdo and Sokolje was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further down is Igman, isn't it? During Mr. Milosevic's time as commander, that largest hill in the surroundings of Sarajevo was in fact held by the BH army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Igman is an enormous mountain. I'm not sure if it was under the control of the BH army in its entirety, or, for that matter, which parts the army of Republika Srpska controlled. Igman is to the west of Sarajevo and it overlooks the general area. But I have no idea who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude by asking this: If Trebevic is near Sarajevo - it's about 1.000 metres high - and Trebevic was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska and Colina Kapa on that same side - just slightly smaller, about 940 metres high - was the only place overlooking Sarajevo that was under the control -- if Trebevic, above Colina Kapa, is the only place under the control of the army of Republika Srpska and all the other hills overlooking Sarajevo are under the control of the BH army, and these run along the confrontation lines, could we put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you can put. I told you, I don't know where the positions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will be established in the course of this trial. But you have already provided sufficient confirmation for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for allowing me the time to complete my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just a few things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 138, just to be clear, the CSB or the centre for security forces, was that a military or a civilian institution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the security services centre. I think you used a different phrase. It's security services centre. I was a civilian police officer. I still am. I wear no uniform. My job was the kind of job done in plain clothes. There were some other members who wore uniforms. That was the uniformed police. They were armed with pistols and some had automatic weapons at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "the uniformed police," are you referring to military combat uniform or police uniform? And what colour was the uniform they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-138 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning they wore standard issue police uniforms. Later on, as I said in my evidence, we received different uniforms, a new set of uniforms, because we had run out of the old ones. I had this uniform; I wasn't compelled to wear it throughout. I was free to choose whether I would wear my civilian clothes or the uniform that we were provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
